historical_timeline.summary: Born in Port Arthur, Texas; the family moves to Beaumont in 1915.
Wins two gold medals and a silver medal in track and field at the Los Angeles Olympic Games.
Voted Associated Press Woman Athlete of the Half-Century, a year after co-founding the LPGA; about this time she buys the Tampa Golf and Country Club and lives there.
Extremely fatigued by the end of the golf season.
Diagnosed with cancer in April 1953; operation including a colostomy in Beaumont.
Wins the U.S. Women's Open by twelve strokes, 14 months after the operation.
The cancer returns; she re-enters John Sealy Hospital in Galveston in June and sets up a cancer fund with her husband in September.
Dies of cancer at John Sealy Hospital in Galveston at 45.

synthetic_episode.teaching_objective: Recognize early-onset rectal cancer in a fit woman of 41, below the screening age, whose rectal bleeding and change in bowel habit could be put down to hemorrhoids, and care for it on the NCCN rectal cancer guideline and the ASCO guidance on locally advanced rectal cancer: a digital rectal examination and prompt colonoscopy with biopsy; mismatch repair testing of every colorectal cancer; germline genetic testing because she is under 50; staging by pelvic MRI and CT, with CEA; a multidisciplinary tumor board; and, because the tumor is mismatch repair deficient, PD-1 blockade with dostarlimab and a watch-and-wait strategy after a clinical complete response, sparing her the abdominoperineal resection and permanent colostomy that a tumor this low would otherwise need. The episode also covers immune-related adverse events (hypothyroidism), iron deficiency anemia, sexual health and body image, return to elite sport, screening of first-degree relatives, the USPSTF screening age of 45, and survivorship care, set against her documented operation with a permanent colostomy in 1953 and her return to win a national championship afterwards.

hpi.narrative: Ms. Didrikson Zaharias returns two weeks after her first visit. Colonoscopy three days after that visit found an ulcerated mass in the lower rectum, from 4 to 9 cm from the anal verge, and nothing else in the colon; the biopsies show adenocarcinoma, and the tumor has lost the mismatch repair proteins MSH2 and MSH6 and is microsatellite instability high. Rectal-protocol MRI shows a tumor whose lower edge is about 1 cm above the anorectal junction, growing just through the bowel wall, with two suspicious lymph nodes and a clear mesorectal fascia (cT3bN1). CT of the chest, abdomen and pelvis shows no spread. The tumor board met three days ago. She was seen today by Dr. Albright-Nakamura and by the colorectal surgeon, who explained that surgery for a tumor this low would most likely mean removing the rectum and anus with a permanent colostomy. She still passes some bright red blood most days, less than before, and feels tired on the back nine. Her first question was whether she would need a bag; her second was whether she could keep playing.

assessment_plan.assessment: Rectal cancer diagnosed two weeks after she first came, because the bleeding in a woman of 41 was examined and scoped at once rather than treated as hemorrhoids. assessment_plan.display: Low rectal adenocarcinoma, mismatch repair deficient, on dostarlimab
assessment_plan.assessment: An early clinical response after one dose: the bleeding has stopped, the tumor is smaller to the finger, and CEA has fallen from 5.8 to 3.4 ng/mL. consultant_note.history: Ms. Didrikson Zaharias, 41, is seen at the request of Dr. Vasquez-Thornbury two weeks after she presented with three months of rectal bleeding, a change in bowel habit and a rectal mass. Since then she has had a colonoscopy with biopsy, rectal-protocol MRI, CT of the chest, abdomen and pelvis, and review at our colorectal tumor board. She still passes a little bright red blood most days, with urgency, and tires late in a round. She has pain during sex and spotting afterwards. She is fully active (ECOG 0), has a levonorgestrel IUD and is not planning a pregnancy. She was seen by the colorectal surgeon this morning. She asked whether she would need a colostomy and whether she could keep playing
consultant_note.data_reviewed: Dr. Vasquez-Thornbury's intake note and results. Colonoscopy: ulcerated mass on the posterior and left wall of the lower rectum, 4 to 9 cm from the anal verge, about half the circumference; the rest of the colon normal. Pathology: adenocarcinoma, moderately differentiated; loss of MSH2 and MSH6 on immunohistochemistry with MLH1 and PMS2 retained; microsatellite instability high. Rectal-protocol MRI: tumor extending 4 mm beyond the muscularis propria (cT3b), two irregular 7 mm mesorectal nodes (cN1), mesorectal fascia clear by 6 mm, no extramural venous invasion, lower edge about 1 cm above the anorectal junction, sphincters not involved. CT of the chest, abdomen and pelvis: no metastases. CEA 5.8 ng/mL at the first visit. Today: hemoglobin 11.1 g/dL, platelets 405, creatinine 0.76 mg/dL, ALT 17 and AST 20 U/L, glucose 90 mg/dL, TSH 1.9 mIU/L, free T4 1.2 ng/dL; urine pregnancy test negative

exam.finding: Fit and composed; weight 62.6 kg; blood pressure 116/72, pulse 80; ECOG 0
Soft, non-tender; no liver enlargement
No inguinal or supraclavicular nodes
Firm, ulcerated mass on the posterior and left wall, lower edge about 4 to 5 cm from the anal verge; normal sphincter tone

assessment.display: Low rectal adenocarcinoma, mismatch repair deficient, cT3bN1M0 (stage IIIB)
assessment.assessment: Locally advanced adenocarcinoma of the low rectum with no distant spread. For a mismatch repair-proficient tumor at this level the standard would be total neoadjuvant therapy (chemoradiation and chemotherapy) followed by total mesorectal excision, and because the lower edge is only about 1 cm above the anorectal junction the operation would most likely be an abdominoperineal resection with a permanent colostomy. This tumor is mismatch repair deficient, which changes everything: in the dostarlimab trial every patient with this kind of tumor who completed six months of treatment had a clinical complete response, and in the larger follow-up study nearly all kept their rectum without radiation or surgery, with few regrowths. The NCCN and ASCO guidelines now recommend checkpoint inhibitor immunotherapy for mismatch repair-deficient locally advanced rectal cancer. The aim is cure with the rectum and sphincter preserved; radiation and surgery remain available if the response is incomplete or the tumor regrows

assessment.display: Iron deficiency anemia from blood loss
assessment.assessment: From the tumor's bleeding; oral iron is enough while the bleeding settles with treatment

recommendations: Dostarlimab 500 mg intravenously every three weeks for nine doses (six months), starting next week

Restaging with rectal-protocol MRI, flexible sigmoidoscopy and digital rectal examination after about three months and again after the last dose, with CT of the chest, abdomen and pelvis at the end; CEA at each restaging

If there is a clinical complete response at the end of treatment, watch-and-wait: examination and sigmoidoscopy every three to four months and MRI every six months for two years, CEA every three to six months, CT every six to twelve months, and colonoscopy at one year
If the response is incomplete, chemoradiation and total mesorectal excision, with stoma site marking and teaching by the wound-ostomy nurse before any operation; no stoma preparation is needed now

Germline multigene panel after genetic counseling, because she is under 50 and the tumor is mismatch repair deficient; if negative, tumor sequencing for somatic MSH2 or MSH6 variants. Her first-degree relatives should start colonoscopy at 40, or 10 years before her age at diagnosis if earlier, every five years, with more intensive Lynch syndrome surveillance only if a germline variant is found
Before the first dose: hepatitis B, hepatitis C and HIV screening, a pregnancy test, and baseline TSH, free T4, liver and kidney tests and glucose

During treatment, primary care to watch for immune-related adverse events, the commonest being thyroid inflammation: TSH and free T4 every six weeks, liver and kidney tests and glucose before each dose, and same-day review for diarrhea, blood in the stool, rash, cough, breathlessness, headache, thirst or unusual tiredness
Oral iron for the anemia, with a blood count in four weeks

She can keep training and competing; dostarlimab does not limit exercise. Contraception with her IUD during treatment and for four months after the last dose; dostarlimab is not known to harm fertility. Sexual pain and spotting should settle as the tumor responds
Distress screening at each visit; she decides who receives these notes
consultant_note.communication: Discussed with Dr. Vasquez-Thornbury and presented at the colorectal tumor board with colorectal surgery, radiation oncology, radiology, pathology and genetics. The images, the biopsy and the meaning of mismatch repair deficiency were explained to Ms. Didrikson Zaharias in plain words, including that surgery would most likely mean a permanent colostomy and that immunotherapy offers a good chance of avoiding it. She chose dostarlimab with watch-and-wait if the response is complete. She decides who else receives this note
